newsitem.title: USA: Wal-Mart limiting sales of cold and diet products.
newsitem.headline: Wal-Mart limiting sales of cold and diet products.

text.p: Wal-Mart Stores Inc. is limiting sales of some allergy, cold and diet products to curtail the illicit manufacture of stimulants that are causing a growing drug problem, the Drug Enforcement Agency said Tuesday.

The agency said in a statement that Wal-Mart, the nation's largest retailer, had programmed the cash registers in its 2,300 retail stores around the country to limit sales of the over-the-counter products to three-to-six packages per customer.
This should help control large-scale purchases of three products -- pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, and phenylpropanolamine, the statement said.

Those products are used in the clandestine manufacture of methamphetamine and amphetamine. The drugs are increasingly attractive to casual drug abusers in the United States, with the greatest problem among methamphetamines, the agency said.

"Wal-Mart, the nation's largest employer, is setting an example of community concern by implementing a chain-wide policy limiting the sales of these allergy, cold and diet products," DEA Administrator Thomas Constantine said in the statement.
"Cold and allergy sufferers, as well as dieters, will not be inconvenienced or harmed and should not see any changes in making their purchases in Wal-Mart stores," Constantine said.
Methamphetamine is known on the street as "crank," ice," and "speed," and is quickly becoming the growth drug of the 1990s, the DEA statement said.

It said methamphetamine results in the same addiction cycle and physiological trauma associated with crack cocaine, but has been called "poor man's cocaine" because it is cheaper and provides a longer-lasting high than cocaine.
Methamphetamine and amphetamine are produced in clandestine labs in the United States and Mexico, the DEA said.

Wal-Mart's action anticipated a new federal regulation that will go into effect in October controlling sales of the products, but the retailer's new limits are much more stringent than the regulation, the DEA said.
Dale Ingram, a spokesman for Wal-Mart, said the sales limits had gone into effect over the last few days and Wal-Mart hoped other retailers would follow suit.
"The more that do this the more deterrent it will be to drug dealers. They are obviously getting bulk purchases from somewhere, but we want to make sure it's not Wal-Mart," Ingram said.
